meta.titre: Immediate Inference and Oppositions: reading the square of opposition and changing the form of a statement
meta.sous_theme: Square of opposition, conversion, obversion and contraposition

sections.contenu_markdown: A radio presenter in Yaoundé claims that all the taxi drivers in the town are honest. A listener phones in with one story of a dishonest driver and says the claim is refuted. Is the listener right, and what else can be said about the other statements built from the same two terms? Questions of this kind come back regularly in Paper 1 and Paper 3 of A Level Philosophy, because from one categorical statement you must be able to infer the truth or falsity of others without a second premise. This course gives you the two tools: the square of opposition and the three changes of form.

items: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false.
A categorical proposition relates two classes, called the subject term and the predicate term.
Quantity is universal or particular, and quality is affirmative or negative.
An immediate inference draws a conclusion from one premise only.

sections.titre: The square of opposition and the immediate inferences
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Standard form
Every categorical statement has a quantifier, a subject term $S$, a copula and a predicate term $P$. There are four standard forms:

| Form | Statement | Quantity | Quality |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | All $S$ are $P$ | universal | affirmative |
| E | No $S$ are $P$ | universal | negative |
| I | Some $S$ are $P$ | particular | affirmative |
| O | Some $S$ are not $P$ | particular | negative |

"Some" means at least one. A singular statement such as "Ngu is a student" is treated as a universal one.

### The square of opposition
The traditional square assumes that the terms name classes that have members.

| Relation | Pair | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Contradictories | A and O, E and I | Always opposite truth values: if one is true the other is false, and if one is false the other is true. |
| Contraries | A and E | Not both true, but both may be false. A true makes E false; A false leaves E undetermined. |
| Subcontraries | I and O | Not both false, but both may be true. I false makes O true; I true leaves O undetermined. |
| Subalternation | A to I, E to O | Truth passes down, falsity passes up. A true makes I true; I false makes A false. A false or I true leaves the other undetermined. |

Contradictories rest on the laws of non-contradiction and excluded middle. The modern (Boolean) interpretation allows empty classes and keeps only the contradictories.

### Changes of form
Each operation gives a new statement from one premise.

| Operation | Rule | A | E | I | O |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Obversion | change the quality and replace the predicate by its complement | No $S$ are non-$P$ | All $S$ are non-$P$ | Some $S$ are not non-$P$ | Some $S$ are non-$P$ |
| Conversion | swap subject and predicate | Some $P$ are $S$ (limitation) | No $P$ are $S$ | Some $P$ are $S$ | no valid converse |
| Contraposition | swap and complement both terms | All non-$P$ are non-$S$ | Some non-$P$ are not non-$S$ (limitation) | no valid contrapositive | Some non-$P$ are not non-$S$ |

Obversion is valid for all four forms and gives an equivalent statement. Limitation means that the quantity is reduced from universal to particular, so the new statement is weaker than the premise.

variantes.nom: Question on the square: given one truth value, find the others
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a statement is declared true or false and you must say what follows for its contrary, subcontrary, contradictory or subaltern.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
1. Put the statement in standard form and name its letter (A, E, I or O).
2. Name the relation asked for (contradictory, contrary, subcontrary or subaltern) and write the new statement in full.
3. Apply the rule of that relation and answer with one of three words: true, false or undetermined.
4. When the question chains several steps, take one step at a time and write each intermediate statement before moving on.

variantes.nom: Question on conversion, obversion and contraposition
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are asked for the converse, the obverse or the contrapositive of a given statement.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find the letter first, because the allowed operations depend on it. Write the complement of a term with "non-" and never forget it in obversion and contraposition. Obversion always works. Conversion fails for O, and contraposition fails for I. When the rule says limitation, the result is particular, and you must say that the new statement does not return you to the original one.

sections.enonce_markdown: It is given that the statement "All the traders in this market are honest persons" is false. (a) State the truth value of its contradictory, its contrary and its subaltern. (b) Write the obverse of the contradictory. (6 marks)

etapes.action: Put the given statement in standard form.
etapes.justification: You cannot apply the square until you know the letter and the two terms.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $S$ = traders in this market, $P$ = honest persons. The statement is A: "All $S$ are $P$". It is false.

etapes.justification: A and O are contradictories, so they always have opposite truth values.
etapes.resultat_markdown: O: "Some traders in this market are not honest persons". Since A is false, O is **true**.

etapes.justification: Contraries cannot both be true but may both be false, so a false A tells you nothing sure about E.
etapes.resultat_markdown: E: "No traders in this market are honest persons". Its truth value is **undetermined**.

etapes.justification: Truth passes from the universal to the particular, but falsity does not.
etapes.resultat_markdown: I: "Some traders in this market are honest persons". A false leaves I **undetermined**.

etapes.justification: Obversion changes the quality and complements the predicate, and the result is equivalent to O, so it is true as well.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Obverse of O: "Some traders in this market are non-honest persons", that is, dishonest persons. It is **true**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer: the contradictory (O) is true; the contrary (E) and the subaltern (I) are undetermined; the obverse of the contradictory is "Some traders in this market are non-honest persons", which is true. The listener in the radio story is therefore right: one dishonest driver is enough to make the universal claim false.

items.erreur_markdown: Given "All $S$ are $P$" is false, the student writes that "No $S$ are $P$" is true.
items.pourquoi_faux: Contraries cannot both be true, but they can both be false. The falsity of A only proves that at least one S is not P.
items.correction_markdown: E is undetermined. The only statement that becomes certain is the contradictory, O: "Some $S$ are not $P$" is true.

items.erreur_markdown: Given "Some $S$ are $P$" is true, the student writes that "Some $S$ are not $P$" is false.
items.pourquoi_faux: I and O are subcontraries: they cannot both be false, but they may both be true.
items.correction_markdown: O is undetermined. If I were false, then O would be true.

items.erreur_markdown: The student converts "All $S$ are $P$" into "All $P$ are $S$".
items.pourquoi_faux: This reverses a one-way relation. All Cameroonian cocoa farmers are farmers, but not all farmers are cocoa farmers.
items.correction_markdown: The valid converse of A is by limitation: "Some $P$ are $S$".

items.erreur_markdown: The student obverts "All $S$ are $P$" into "No $S$ are $P$".
items.pourquoi_faux: Only the quality was changed. Changing quality without complementing the predicate gives the contrary, not the obverse.
items.correction_markdown: The obverse is "No $S$ are non-$P$": both the quality changes and the predicate is replaced by its complement.

items.erreur_markdown: Given "All $S$ are $P$" is false, the student writes that "Some $S$ are $P$" is false too.
items.pourquoi_faux: Falsity passes up from the particular to the universal, not down. A false universal can still have true instances.
items.correction_markdown: I is undetermined when A is false. Only a false I would force A to be false.

items.enonce_markdown: The statement "Some prefects in the school are girls" is false. State the truth value of the A, E and O statements formed from the same terms and name the relation used each time.
items.solution_markdown:
Let $S$ = prefects in the school and $P$ = girls. The given statement is I and it is false.
- A, "All prefects in the school are girls": **false**, by subalternation (the falsity of the particular passes up to the universal).
- E, "No prefects in the school are girls": **true**, because E is the contradictory of I.
- O, "Some prefects in the school are not girls": **true**, because I and O are subcontraries and cannot both be false.

items.enonce_markdown: Write the obverse, the converse and the contrapositive of "All cocoa farmers in the village are members of the cooperative". Say which of the three is not equivalent to the original statement.
items.solution_markdown:
Let $S$ = cocoa farmers in the village and $P$ = members of the cooperative.
- Obverse: "No cocoa farmers in the village are non-members of the cooperative" (equivalent).
- Converse, by limitation: "Some members of the cooperative are cocoa farmers in the village" (weaker, not equivalent).
- Contrapositive: "All non-members of the cooperative are non-cocoa-farmers in the village" (equivalent).
The statement that is not equivalent to the original is the **converse**.

items.enonce_markdown: The statement "Some roads in the town are not tarred" is true. (a) State the contradictory and its truth value. (b) State the contrary of that contradictory and its truth value. (c) State the subcontrary of the given statement and its truth value. (d) Write the obverse of the statement found in (c).
items.solution_markdown:
Let $S$ = roads in the town and $P$ = tarred roads. The given statement is O and it is true.
(a) The contradictory is A, "All roads in the town are tarred": **false**.
(b) The contrary of A is E, "No roads in the town are tarred". A is false, so E is **undetermined**.
(c) The subcontrary of O is I, "Some roads in the town are tarred": **undetermined**, because subcontraries can both be true and a true O leaves I open.
(d) The obverse of I is "Some roads in the town are not untarred roads" (not non-tarred roads), which is equivalent to I, so its truth value is also **undetermined**.

items_markdown: The four standard forms are A (all), E (no), I (some) and O (some are not); name the letter first in every question.
Contradictories (A and O, E and I) always have opposite truth values; contraries cannot both be true; subcontraries cannot both be false.
Truth passes down from the universal to the subaltern and falsity passes up; the other directions are undetermined.
Obversion is valid for all four forms; conversion fails for O; contraposition fails for I; limitation weakens the result.
Answer with true, false or undetermined, and write each intermediate statement in full to earn the method marks.
